paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the objective is the average reward earned over continuing interaction. It considers general policy parametrization and asks how quickly an actor-critic method can converge globally. Previous guarantees face several obstacles: unfavorable dependence on the number of states and actions, many required iterations, or substantial reliance on knowledge of mixing and hitting times.

The proposed algorithm, MLMC-NAC, combines a natural actor-critic approach with multilevel Monte Carlo. The central contribution is a sharper convergence analysis for this combination. The authors establish a global convergence rate proportional to one over the square root of the interaction horizon, with logarithmic factors suppressed. They identify this as the first actor-critic guarantee of that order for average-reward Markov decision processes.

A particularly consequential feature is that the stated rate does not grow with the size of the state space. This makes the analysis applicable even to infinite state spaces. The result concerns a theoretical convergence guarantee, explaining how the proposed approach improves the scaling of guarantees for this learning objective.
icml-2025-a-sharper-global-convergence-a.tldr: MLMC-NAC achieves a sharper global convergence guarantee for average-reward reinforcement learning without dependence on state-space size.

paragraphs: AnalogGenie-Lite addresses the search for new analog integrated-circuit topologies: the patterns of connections that define a circuit. The motivation is that improvements from shrinking semiconductor technology are slowing, making new circuit structures an increasingly important route to better performance. The paper focuses on making automated topology discovery more scalable and more likely to produce valid results.

The method uses a decoder-only transformer with a lightweight graph representation. Its contributions include a concise representation of device pins, mining frequently occurring subgraphs, and sequence modeling. The device-pin representation changes the stated complexity from quadratic to linear. This representation change is central to the approach because it reduces how quickly the description grows as the represented structure becomes larger.

Compared with existing leading topology-discovery methods, the authors report scalability gains of 5.15 to 71.11 times and validity improvements of 23.5% to 33.6%. These findings support the value of changing how circuit graphs are represented for generation. Additional case studies on graphs from other domains suggest broader applicability of the graph-modeling approach.
icml-2025-analoggenie-lite-enhancing-sca.tldr: AnalogGenie-Lite uses compact graph modeling to improve the scalability and validity of transformer-based analog circuit topology discovery.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction provides prediction sets with a target coverage level, but coverage across the population can hide poor coverage for underrepresented groups. Calibrating separately within each protected group addresses this fairness concern. However, small group sample sizes can produce very wide sets, leaving a tension between reliable group coverage and useful precision.

SAGCCI tackles that tension through two complementary ideas. It clusters protected groups whose conformal scores have similar distributions, allowing their information to contribute to more precise inference. It also incorporates surrogate outcomes through an efficient influence function. Together, these components aim to produce tighter prediction sets while preserving the group-level coverage objective.

The theoretical guarantee is approximate group-conditional coverage, with double robustness under mild convergence conditions; it is not an unconditional exact guarantee. Simulations and an analysis of the Moderna COVE vaccine trial show narrower prediction sets than existing methods while maintaining valid group-conditional coverage. The findings indicate that suitable information sharing and surrogate outcomes can improve precision without abandoning the stated fairness target.
icml-2025-bridging-fairness-and-efficien.tldr: SAGCCI combines group clustering and surrogate outcomes to tighten prediction sets while supporting approximate group-conditional coverage.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models need to satisfy several goals together: follow the prompt, produce high-quality images, and match human aesthetic preferences. Preference alignment and guidance during generation both contribute to these goals. This paper argues that treating training-time alignment and generation-time sampling independently leaves useful opportunities for cooperation unexplored.

CHATS connects these stages by separately modeling distributions of preferred and dispreferred outputs. It then uses a sampling strategy based on proxy prompts to draw useful information from both distributions. The distinctive idea is that dispreferred outputs also provide information for generation, rather than serving only as examples to discourage during alignment. The framework makes this information part of the sampling process.

The authors report strong performance from a small, high-quality fine-tuning dataset, suggesting substantial data efficiency in their experiments. Across standard benchmarks, CHATS surpasses traditional preference-alignment methods and achieves reported state-of-the-art results. These findings support coordinating how a model learns human preferences with how it generates images, rather than evaluating either component only in isolation.
icml-2025-chats-combining-human-aligned-.tldr: CHATS coordinates preference learning and sampling, using preferred and dispreferred distributions to improve text-to-image generation with little fine-tuning data.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks which connections are missing from a network. Many approaches assume that enough links are already visible to learn from, but sparse observations make this difficult. This paper uses hierarchical modularity—the organization of connections into nested groups—as a prior structure that can remain useful even when relatively few links are observed.

The authors introduce complete-tree space, a discrete metric space designed to express this hierarchy and its permutation symmetries. They use group theory to compare those symmetries with ones in other spaces. Their analysis establishes a substantially lower bound on sample complexity for complete-tree space than for the commonly used Euclidean space, connecting the representation's structure to the paper's data-efficiency argument.

The accompanying algorithm, leaf matching, embeds network nodes in complete-tree space and turns discrete optimization into decentralized search. Experiments support the data efficiency of this space relative to alternatives. Leaf matching also outperforms a leading graph transformer when data are scarce and shows strong scalability, suggesting that a hierarchy-oriented representation can be valuable when observed connections are limited.
icml-2025-complete-tree-space-favors-dat.tldr: Complete-tree space encodes network hierarchies to support data-efficient link prediction, with leaf matching performing well when observed links are scarce.

paragraphs: LoRA fine-tuning creates specialized versions of a language model through relatively small parameter updates. Serving a large collection still presents a memory problem: requests may require different updates, and thousands of adapters cannot all fit in GPU memory. Continually moving adapters into and out of memory therefore remains a bottleneck even in optimized serving systems.

This paper addresses the bottleneck by compressing adapters jointly. It represents them using a shared basis together with scaling matrices specific to each adapter. The method also learns clusters of adapters that can be compressed effectively together. Clustering allows the approach to handle large collections without requiring every adapter to share the same compression structure.

The authors report experiments with up to 1,000 adapters in which compression preserves performance. They also report substantial throughput improvements in realistic serving scenarios involving more than a thousand adapters, reaching 80% of single-adapter serving throughput. The result shows how exploiting shared structure across adaptations can reduce the serving overhead associated with supporting many specialized versions of one model.
icml-2025-compress-then-serve-serving-th.tldr: Jointly compressing LoRA adapters into shared bases reduces serving overhead while preserving performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning seeks high rewards while respecting limits on costly or unsafe behavior. Yet an agent can violate those limits during training. This paper identifies underestimating the cost value function as an important contributor: if predicted costs are too low, the learner can treat risky behavior as more acceptable than it really is.

MICE addresses this problem with a memory of previously explored unsafe states. That memory identifies high-cost regions, and a pseudo-count associated with visits to those regions defines an additional intrinsic cost. The method combines this signal with the external cost in a cost value function and applies bias correction. It then uses that function to formulate a trust-region optimization objective and corresponding update methods.

The theoretical analysis provides convergence guarantees for the proposed cost value function and a worst-case constraint-violation result for the update. Experiments show substantially fewer constraint violations while maintaining policy performance comparable to baselines. The contribution is therefore a method for reducing unsafe exploration through better cost estimation, with both theoretical analysis and empirical support.
icml-2025-controlling-underestimation-bi.tldr: MICE remembers unsafe states and corrects cost estimates to reduce training-time constraint violations while preserving comparable policy performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find a feasible action when the linear constraints defining feasibility are unknown. A learner tries actions and observes noisy constraint measurements. Its goal is either to identify infeasibility or to find an action with a nearly optimal safety margin, meaning a favorable signed distance from the constraint boundary.

The proposed FAST algorithm extends Thompson sampling to this setting with multiple objectives. It applies a coupled random perturbation to the estimated constraint matrix and chooses a maximin action in the resulting game. Coupling the perturbations is a central technical contribution, alongside an analysis that avoids relying on convexity considerations.

The authors prove stopping-time and safety-cost guarantees that depend on action dimension and the optimal safety margin, with stopping time also depending on requested accuracy. FAST additionally supplies an initialization for existing safe linear-bandit methods. Combining them yields the stated regret guarantee and constant-order risk without prior knowledge of a safe action. This addresses a practical gap in methods that otherwise need safety to be established before learning begins.
icml-2025-feasible-action-search-for-ban.tldr: FAST uses coupled Thompson sampling to find a nearly maximally safe feasible action or detect infeasibility from noisy observations.

paragraphs: This paper builds generalized additive models from ensembles of axis-aligned decision stumps. Stumps that use the same input feature are grouped into that feature's shape function. This organization expresses the overall prediction through separate feature contributions, while allowing each contribution to be assembled from multiple simple decision rules.

The authors learn a fixed-size forest through alternating optimization instead of boosting or bagging. With the other stumps held fixed, they optimize each stump exactly by enumerating possibilities. Once the split choices are fixed, they optimize all leaf values together by solving a convex problem. These are exact solutions to particular subproblems within the alternating procedure, rather than a stated global guarantee for the whole training problem.

Naively optimizing stump forests can overfit, so the paper introduces regularization techniques to control that behavior. The resulting models achieve accuracy comparable to leading generalized additive models while using fewer parameters. The findings show that direct, regularized optimization can successfully train these forests, offering a different route from the traditional ensemble-building procedures.
icml-2025-generalized-additive-models-vi.tldr: Directly optimizing regularized stump forests produces generalized additive models with competitive accuracy and fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Gradient Boosting Reinforcement Learning brings boosted trees into a setting usually dominated by neural networks. The motivation is that structured observations, categorical features, and irregular relationships can be difficult for neural networks, while boosted trees have strengths on these kinds of data in supervised learning. Applying those strengths to reinforcement learning requires changing how training proceeds.

Traditional gradient-boosting libraries assume a static dataset with fixed labels. Reinforcement learning instead changes the data encountered and the learning signals as interaction continues. GBRL handles this mismatch by repeatedly interleaving tree construction with environment interaction. The framework therefore adapts tree learning to an evolving learning process rather than treating the experience as one fixed supervised dataset.

Experiments show GBRL outperforming neural networks in domains with structured observations and categorical features, while remaining competitive on standard continuous-control benchmarks. The authors also report stronger robustness to out-of-distribution samples and better handling of irregular state-action relationships. These findings support boosted trees as a useful reinforcement-learning model family, particularly where the observation structure suits their strengths.
icml-2025-gradient-boosting-reinforcemen.tldr: GBRL adapts boosted trees to ongoing environment interaction, improving results on structured and categorical reinforcement-learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies private model training when a single training example can belong to several users. It calls this the multi-attribution setting and develops a user-level differential-privacy definition for it. The central issue is that controlling one person's contribution becomes more complicated when examples are shared across people rather than attributed to only one user.

The authors formulate contribution bounding as a dataset-selection problem: choose a subset in which each user is associated with only a limited number of examples. They propose a greedy baseline and examine variants that optimize the selected subset using different techniques and criteria. This makes the selection step a concrete part of enabling private training under shared attribution.

Experiments cover a synthetic logistic-regression task and a transformer-training task. The simple greedy algorithm remains competitive with its variants in most settings. The study also identifies the practical importance of a bias-variance tradeoff in contribution bounding. Its findings suggest that selecting a privacy-compatible subset requires attention to statistical effects, beyond simply enforcing the per-user contribution limit.
icml-2025-its-my-data-too-private-ml-for.tldr: The paper defines user-level privacy for shared training examples and studies greedy contribution bounding as a practical training ingredient.

paragraphs: Machine-learning interatomic potentials approximate quantum-mechanical calculations at much lower computational cost. However, better accuracy on held-out examples does not always lead to better predictions of physical properties. This paper investigates that mismatch by asking whether a learned potential behaves appropriately during molecular-dynamics simulation, where its predictions are used repeatedly as the system evolves.

The proposed practical check is whether the model conserves energy during those simulations. Among models that pass this test, the authors find a stronger relationship between held-out prediction errors and downstream physical-property performance. Passing the check therefore helps make test error more informative in their study; it does not establish that lower error alone guarantees better results.

The authors identify modeling choices that may cause failures of the energy-conservation test and use those observations to improve highly expressive potentials. The resulting model, eSEN, achieves reported state-of-the-art results for materials stability, thermal conductivity, and phonon calculations. The work connects model development to physical behavior in simulation, making that behavior part of evaluating whether predictive accuracy translates into useful scientific results.
icml-2025-learning-smooth-and-expressive.tldr: Energy-conservation testing guides the development of eSEN and makes test errors more informative about downstream physical-property predictions.

paragraphs: This paper considers regression subject to demographic parity, a fairness constraint. The objective is to achieve the strongest possible predictive accuracy while satisfying that constraint. Earlier work established fair minimax-optimal methods, but its analyses were closely tied to particular models of how the data were generated, making the conclusions specific to those settings.

The authors develop meta-theorems that can validate fair minimax optimality across a variety of situations. These results provide a reusable level of analysis: instead of deriving every fairness-constrained regression result entirely around one data-generation model, researchers can apply broader theorems to the corresponding algorithms. Minimax optimality concerns the best worst-case accuracy within the setting being analyzed.

The paper also shows that post-processing can achieve fair minimax-optimal regression. This makes improvements to conventional regression methods relevant to fair regression, because their outputs can subsequently be adapted to the constraint. The contribution is a theoretical basis for this workflow, allowing predictive modeling and fairness adaptation to be developed as connected stages.
icml-2025-meta-optimality-for-demographi.tldr: Reusable meta-theorems show how post-processing can achieve minimax-optimal regression under demographic parity.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate outputs through iterative sampling, which can make generation computationally expensive. This paper examines two acceleration strategies, caching and quantization, and studies how their computational errors affect generation quality. Its starting point is that accelerating the repeated computation requires managing the errors introduced by those shortcuts.

The proposed framework, Modulated Diffusion or MoDiff, combines modulated quantization with error compensation. It is designed to retain advantages of existing caching and quantization approaches while addressing their limitations. The authors support the framework with theoretical analysis and present it as generally applicable to diffusion models, connecting acceleration to explicit treatment of approximation error.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and LSUN show activation quantization reduced from eight bits to three bits without performance degradation in the reported post-training-quantization setting. This is the concrete empirical result behind the method's promise: substantially lower activation precision can remain compatible with generation quality when accompanied by the proposed modulation and compensation. The reported evidence establishes that outcome on the evaluated datasets.
icml-2025-modulated-diffusion-accelerati.tldr: MoDiff combines modulated quantization and error compensation, enabling three-bit activations without reported performance loss on CIFAR-10 and LSUN.

paragraphs: Multi-object tracking must maintain an object's identity as it moves, including periods when other objects hide it. MOTE addresses this occlusion problem by combining deformable detection transformers with a custom disocclusion matrix. Its aim is to preserve track consistency by estimating the motion of objects even when direct visual evidence temporarily disappears.

The method uses optical flow to generate features, which pass through a softmax splatting layer to help construct the disocclusion matrix. It also modifies an enhanced track embedding module so these features enter the track-query embeddings. This connects motion information to the representations used for tracking, allowing the model to predict trajectories through periods of occlusion.

Evaluation on MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack reports better results than existing leading methods across all tested benchmarks. For example, MOTE reaches 82.0 MOTA and 66.3 HOTA on MOT17. The authors particularly emphasize fewer identity switches and more consistent tracking in scenes with frequent occlusions. These findings support incorporating estimated hidden-object motion directly into the tracking architecture.
icml-2025-more-than-meets-the-eye-enhanc.tldr: MOTE integrates motion-derived disocclusion features into transformer tracking to preserve object identities through occlusion.

paragraphs: Distributional compositional generalization concerns solving tasks from new distributions by combining concepts learned from supporting distributions. This paper studies the statistical mechanisms behind that ability. It asks whether a method for one such problem can apply to another, and which statistical properties reveal an algorithm's capacity to compose knowledge.

For the first question, the authors propose an invariant measure that provides a common dimension for comparing different methods. Their analysis highlights the role of data in enabling improvements without trade-offs. The measure supplies a shared statistical perspective on approaches that might otherwise be studied separately for their particular compositional tasks.

For the second question, the analysis separates the effect of insufficient data from the effect of knowledge composition itself. After making that distinction, it connects compositional ability to compatibility and sensitivity between the learning algorithm and the composition rule. This helps clarify why evaluating composition requires considering both available data and the relationship between the learner and the way knowledge must be combined.
icml-2025-on-the-statistical-mechanisms-.tldr: The paper develops a statistical account of compositional generalization that separates data scarcity from algorithm–composition compatibility.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns how well a classifier's confidence agrees with its predictive reliability. A common way to evaluate it groups predictions into equal-width confidence bins. However, theoretical analysis of the bias introduced by this grouping has largely focused on binary classification, leaving a gap for multiclass applications. Many parametric recalibration methods also lack guarantees about performance on new data.

This paper uses the PAC-Bayes framework to analyze the generalization of calibration error. The authors derive what they identify as the first optimizable upper bound on generalization error in this calibration setting. An optimizable bound matters because it can inform how a recalibration procedure is trained, rather than merely describing its behavior afterward.

Using this theory, the authors propose a recalibration algorithm that explicitly accounts for generalization. Numerical experiments show improvements to Gaussian-process-based recalibration across multiple benchmark datasets and models. The contribution therefore connects theoretical analysis with a usable adjustment procedure, addressing whether improvements in calibration extend beyond the data used to fit that adjustment.
icml-2025-pac-bayes-analysis-for-recalib.tldr: A PAC-Bayes calibration bound motivates a generalization-aware algorithm that improves Gaussian-process-based recalibration in experiments.

paragraphs: Deep state-space models offer strong language-modeling performance with computation that scales linearly with sequence length. This paper asks how to adapt them using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, an area that has received less attention for these architectures. It examines both which existing methods work well and which parts of the model those methods should target.

The analysis finds that LoRA and its variants consistently outperform the other evaluated parameter-efficient methods. However, their effectiveness differs across components: LoRA works well for linear projection matrices but fails on the state-space modules themselves. Even there, it still outperforms the other applicable methods, highlighting a weakness in the available approaches to adapting those modules.

The authors introduce Sparse Dimension Tuning, a method tailored to state-space modules. They combine it with LoRA on the linear projection matrices, assigning different tuning methods to different architectural components. This combination achieves reported state-of-the-art performance across extensive experiments. The findings emphasize that choosing where and how to adapt parameters is central to effective fine-tuning of state-space models.
icml-2025-parameter-efficient-fine-tunin.tldr: Sparse Dimension Tuning adapts state-space modules while LoRA handles projection matrices, improving parameter-efficient fine-tuning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: PiD detects generated images by focusing on low-level residual signals rather than their visible semantic content. The motivating observation is that generative models prioritize high-level content and can overlook lower-level components. Separating those components aims to expose forgery clues that depend less on what an image depicts and can therefore be useful across different image content.

The extraction procedure operates on individual pixel vectors. It transforms a pixel from RGB into another color space, such as YUV, quantizes the transformed vector, and maps it back into RGB. The loss introduced by quantization becomes the residual used for detection. This provides a direct way to obtain a detection signal without reconstructing the image through a generative model.

The authors describe PiD as computationally efficient relative to prior approaches based on reconstruction or high-frequency information. They report 98% accuracy on the GenImage benchmark, supporting its effectiveness and generalization in that evaluation. The distinctive contribution is a simple pixel-level decomposition designed to make less semantic, more general forgery evidence available to the detector.
icml-2025-pid-generalized-ai-generated-i.tldr: PiD extracts pixelwise quantization residuals to detect generated images, achieving reported accuracy of 98% on GenImage.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether adding more clean preference data always helps align a large language model. Its central proposal is that the usefulness of an example depends on whether the model has enough capacity to learn from it. Examples that are too difficult can hinder alignment, making the match between data and model an important consideration in selecting training data.

The authors investigate this idea through systematic experiments. They find consistent orders in which preference examples are learned across alignment runs, providing evidence that examples differ in difficulty. They also report that overly difficult examples significantly reduce performance across four language models and two datasets. The difficulty threshold a model can handle depends on its capacity, so an example’s suitability is tied to the model being trained.

Using these findings, the authors introduce Selective DPO, which filters out overly difficult preference examples. They report improvements of 9–16% in win rates on AlpacaEval 2 compared with the DPO baseline, along with better results than several DPO variants that change the algorithm. These results support selecting preference data according to model capacity: in the reported experiments, removing examples beyond that capacity improved alignment performance.
icml-2025-principled-data-selection-for-.tldr: Selective DPO improves alignment in the reported experiments by filtering out preference examples that are too difficult for a model’s capacity.

paragraphs: This paper investigates quantum acceleration for reinforcement learning in an unknown Markov decision process with an infinite-horizon average-reward objective. It introduces a framework that extends conventional agent-environment interaction to include quantum signals. That interaction framework is an important part of the setting in which the paper establishes its theoretical advantage.

The proposed algorithm is tabular and driven by optimism. It uses efficient quantum mean estimation to extract information from the available quantum signals. The analysis connects the advantage of quantum mean estimation to improved regret guarantees, where regret measures the reward shortfall accumulated while the agent learns.

The stated bound is constant order up to factors logarithmic in the horizon length, compared with the square-root horizon dependence of the cited classical counterparts. The authors characterize this as an exponential improvement in regret guarantees. Because the notation suppresses logarithmic terms, the result should not be read as strictly constant regret. It is a theoretical improvement under the proposed quantum interaction framework.
icml-2025-quantum-speedups-in-regret-ana.tldr: Under a quantum interaction framework, quantum mean estimation yields average-reward reinforcement-learning regret with only suppressed logarithmic horizon dependence.

paragraphs: Randomized dimensionality reduction can speed up geometric optimization by moving data into a space with fewer coordinates. This paper studies that approach for Euclidean maximization problems, including maximum matching, maximum spanning trees, and measures of dataset diversity. The central question is how many dimensions these tasks require after projection.

The authors show that the answer is closely connected to the dataset's doubling dimension, a measure of its intrinsic dimensionality. The required projected dimension scales linearly with that quantity. They also establish that this dependence is necessary for some of the problems considered. This differs from classical dimension-reduction results whose dimensional requirements grow with the number of data points.

The distinction matters because dataset size and intrinsic geometric complexity describe different aspects of the input. The theory ties compression requirements to the latter for the studied objectives. Empirical results additionally support the quality of solutions obtained in the projected space and demonstrate speedups from dimensionality reduction, connecting the geometric analysis to computational benefits.
icml-2025-randomized-dimensionality-redu.tldr: For several geometric maximization tasks, useful projection dimension scales with intrinsic doubling dimension rather than dataset size.

paragraphs: External slow-thinking methods use additional computation at test time to improve a language model's multistep reasoning. Although these approaches can help, their underlying mechanisms are less well understood. This paper develops a theoretical account centered on snowball errors: the way errors arising during reasoning relate to the eventual chance of reaching a correct result.

The authors use information theory to connect this error effect to the probability of correct reasoning. They then interpret external slow-thinking approaches as different strategies for reducing error probability. A comparative analysis covers methods ranging from simple to complex, describing both their distinctions and the relationships between them within this shared perspective.

The findings suggest that the particular external framework is not the primary determinant of effectiveness. Instead, expanding the search scope or improving the model's internal reasoning capacity may provide more sustained gains over time. This is a qualified conclusion about promising directions, grounded in the paper's analysis, rather than a claim that all frameworks perform identically.
icml-2025-rethinking-external-slow-think.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis interprets external slow-thinking methods as ways to reduce reasoning errors and highlights search scope and model capacity.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks to recover underlying causal factors from observed data. This paper tests representative methods in a controlled optical experiment built specifically for evaluation. The experiment has known causal inputs, providing ground truth, and satisfies core assumptions of causal representation learning. It therefore offers a concrete real-world setting where the evaluated methods are expected to succeed.

All selected methods fail to recover the underlying factors. To investigate why, the authors replace the real data-generating process with a simpler synthetic counterpart. Most methods also fail on this simplified ablation, revealing a reproducibility problem beyond the difficulty of the physical system itself.

The study additionally finds that assumptions about the mixing function are crucial for some methods but do not hold in the real data. This distinguishes satisfying core assumptions from satisfying every method-relevant condition. The benchmark exposes a gap between theoretical promise and practical recovery, and the authors release code and datasets to support further development and validation.
icml-2025-sanity-checking-causal-represe.tldr: Representative causal representation methods fail on a controlled optical benchmark, with synthetic ablations exposing reproducibility and assumption-related problems.

paragraphs: Many graph uncertainty methods work best when connected nodes are similar, a property called homophily. Their performance can deteriorate on heterophilic graphs, where neighbors differ semantically. This paper studies that problem through an information-theoretic analysis of message-passing neural networks, examining what information their layers contain about a node's prediction target.

The authors develop an analogue of the data processing inequality suited to this setting. They show that information about the target can increase with depth when a node's features differ semantically from its neighbors. Consequently, representations at different layers can provide distinct information about the data distribution. This motivates considering those representations together when estimating epistemic uncertainty.

The proposed empirical implementation is a simple density estimator applied after training to the joint space of node embeddings. It achieves reported state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation on heterophilic graphs while matching previous work on homophilic graphs. It does so without post-processing that explicitly exploits homophily, supporting the broader design principle of combining information across layers.
icml-2025-uncertainty-estimation-for-het.tldr: Combining node representations across layers improves uncertainty estimation on heterophilic graphs, supported by information-theoretic analysis and experiments.
